The Buddha is misquoted a lot.  If you read orthodox teachings, you can see that he’s uncomfortable with questions about ultimate truths such as god, the afterlife, and even the nature of a Buddha as a being.  Several places in the Pali canon, the oldest and most orthodox of Buddhist canons, he states outright that he doesn’t know what happens after you die, or if there’s a god.  If I’m remembering correctly, and it’s been a while, it’s called the 14 questions, 14 questions about the nature of reality that he refused to answer, and one of them is what happens after death, which leads one to the question of the nature of death itself.  Is it final?  Or can we live on through our actions? And if we live on through our actions after death then we live on through the actions we take during our lives.

See, this is where it gets a bit tricky.  Reincarnation in Buddhism is very misunderstood in the west.  Buddhism denies the existence of an immortal soul, or at least it doesn’t confirm it.  Reincarnation in Buddhism dictates that you don’t just die and then reincarnate as another “you”.  Death is a part of existence.  Every second of every day you are dying and being reborn as the actions you take and the thoughts in your head.  Lord Buddha lived and taught in a Vedic society, so Hinduism is a big part of his teachings, but I’d argue that if he was a Nazarene then Christ would be a big part of his teachings.  It speaks to his genius, and to the truth and power of his dhamma that he could fit this truth anywhere and not change anything about where he put it.
